column.label: supported
column.says: The site, just outside Selçuk, is marked by a single column built of miscellaneous fragments found here.
quote: Today the site of the temple, which lies just outside Selçuk, is marked by a single column constructed of  miscellaneous fragments discovered at the site.

wonder.label: verified
wonder.says: The Temple of Artemis was one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world; little remains.
quote: Little remains of the famous Temple of Artemis, one of the “Seven Wonders of the World,” which drew pilgrims from all around the Mediterranean.
is considered one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World

diana.label: supported

quote: dedicated to a localised form of the goddess Artemis (equated with the Roman goddess Diana)

flood.label: supported

quote: the earliest version of the temple was destroyed by a flood in the 7th century BC

second.label: supported
second.says: From around 550 BC Chersiphron and his son Metagenes built a new temple, 115 m (377 ft) by 46 m (151 ft), supposedly the first Greek temple of marble, sponsored partly by Croesus.
quote: The new temple was sponsored at least in part by Croesus

It was designed and constructed from around 550 BC by the Greek Cretan architect Chersiphron and his son Metagenes. It was 115 m (377 ft) long and 46 m (151 ft) wide, supposedly the first Greek temple built of marble.

marsh.label: supported
marsh.says: Pliny claims the architects chose marshy ground as a precaution against earthquakes.
quote: Pliny the Elder, seemingly unaware of the ancient continuity of the sacred site, claims that the new temple's architects chose to build it on marshy ground as a precaution against earthquakes

herostratus.label: legend
herostratus.says: In 356 BC the temple burned; sources describe arson by Herostratus seeking fame; the Ephesians executed him and banned his name.
quote: He was then executed.
In 356 BC, the temple burned down. Various sources describe this as an act of arson by Herostratus, who set fire to the wooden roof-beams, seeking fame at any cost
For this outrage, the Ephesians sentenced the perpetrator to death and forbade anyone from mentioning his name, although Theopompus later noted it.

torture.label: supported
torture.says: He confessed his motive under torture.
quote: Promptly arrested, he was tortured on the rack, where he confessed to having committed the arson to secure everlasting fame or notoriety.

doubt.label: disputed
doubt.says: Modern scholars question Herostratus's role; some suggest the temple's own administrators set the fire because the foundation was sinking.
quote: Herostratus' part in the temple's destruction has been questioned in modern scholarship.
The fire might even have been deliberately and covertly set by the temple's administrators, who were aware that the temple's foundation was sinking

eponym.label: supported
eponym.says: His name became a term for someone who commits a crime to become famous.
quote: His name has become an eponym for someone who commits a crime solely to become famous.

alexander-birth.label: tradition
alexander-birth.says: Tradition said the fire coincided with Alexander the Great's birth; Plutarch said Artemis was too busy with the delivery to save her temple.
quote: In Greek and Roman historical tradition, the temple's destruction coincided with the birth of Alexander the Great
Plutarch remarks that Artemis was too preoccupied with Alexander's delivery to save her burning temple.

alexander-offer.label: supported

third.label: supported

quote: Work started in 323 BC and continued for many years. The third temple was larger than the second; 137 m (450 ft) long by 69 m (225 ft) wide and 18 m (60 ft) high, with more than 127 columns.

parts.name: The lone column
parts.stand: On the path at the edge of the field, facing the single tall column.

paras.t: That one column, standing in a marshy field, is nearly all that's left of the Temple of Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world. It's not even an original column: it was put together from fragments found here.
The goddess here was a local form of Artemis, whom the Romans called Diana. Keep that name in mind; we'll meet it again in the Bible.
Notice how wet the ground is. This was always a swampy site, and the high water table has made digging hard.
After rain the ground here can be soft and muddy. Mind your footing.

parts.name: Temples, fire and fame
parts.stand: Stay facing the column and picture a forest of marble columns around it.

paras.t: There were several temples here. An early one was wiped out by a flood in the 7th century BC. From around 550 BC the architect Chersiphron and his son Metagenes built a new one, 377 feet long and 151 feet wide, said to be the first Greek temple built of marble. King Croesus helped pay for it.
The Roman writer Pliny claims they chose this marshy ground on purpose, as a precaution against earthquakes.

In 356 BC the temple here burned. As the story goes, a man named Herostratus set fire to the roof beams for one reason: to be famous. The Ephesians executed him and banned anyone from saying his name. It didn't work. His name became a word for someone who commits a crime just to be known.
Was it really him? Scholars aren't sure. He confessed his motive under torture, and some suggest the temple's own managers may have set the fire, because they knew the foundation was sinking.

Ancient tradition added a flourish: the fire happened on the very day Alexander the Great was born. Plutarch remarks that Artemis was too busy with the delivery to save her temple. Years later Alexander offered to pay for the rebuilding, and the Ephesians tactfully refused. It would be improper, they said, for one god to build a temple to another.

They rebuilt it themselves from 323 BC, even bigger: 450 feet long, 225 wide, 60 feet high, with more than 127 columns. Antipater of Sidon, who drew up a list of the Seven Wonders, wrote that when he saw the house of Artemis, the other wonders lost their brilliancy.

This is the temple behind the riot in the book of Acts. A silversmith named Demetrius made silver shrines for Diana, and he warned the craftsmen that because of Paul, the temple of the great goddess Diana might be despised, whom all Asia and the world worshippeth. They cried out, Great is Diana of the Ephesians.

The town clerk who calmed them asked who did not know that Ephesus was a worshipper of the great goddess Diana, and of the image which fell down from Jupiter. That detail, an image fallen from the sky, is known for this temple from Acts alone.
In the Ephesus Museum in Selçuk you may see her statues, covered in oval shapes. They were long read as many breasts, a sign of fertility. Modern scholars doubt it.

parts.name: How it disappeared
parts.stand: Look around the field at the scattered stones.

paras.t: According to the historian Jordanes, Goths set fire to the temple in 268 AD. How badly it was damaged, nobody knows. Christian writers mention it being closed in the 5th century, and some of its stone was carried off for other buildings.
There's a medieval legend that columns from here hold up the Hagia Sophia in Istanbul. A nice story, but there's no truth to it.
The site was lost so completely that it took an expedition led by John Turtle Wood, for the British Museum, six years of searching to find it again, in 1869.

So here is one of the wonders of the world, reduced to a single column. And as the story goes, a man burned it just to be remembered. Stand here a moment and ask yourself the better question: what would you want to be remembered for?
